# Specific Model Architectures

Also called: NeRF Architectures, Radiance Field Network Variants

## Overview
Specific Model Architectures refers to the family of structural modifications applied to the canonical [Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to address limitations in rendering speed, geometric accuracy, generalization, and robustness to sparse or unconstrained inputs [S1, unofficial][S2]. While the [standard NeRF](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) uses a single deep MLP to map 5D coordinates to density and color, this family encompasses methods that decouple networks, replace MLPs with [voxel grids](#1719-voxel-grid-indexing.md) or image-based projections, integrate convolutional layers, or employ generative frameworks [S1, unofficial][S2, S3]. These architectures are chosen to solve specific problems such as the computational bottleneck of dense sampling, the ambiguity of sparse views, or the inability to generalize across unseen objects [S1, unofficial][S2].

## Shared principles
The canonical [NeRF architecture](#910-nerf-mlp-architecture.md) maps a 3D position $\mathbf{x}$ and viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$ to volume density $\sigma$ and view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}$ using a fully connected MLP [S1, unofficial]. Specific model architectures generally retain the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) as the output mechanism:
$$ C(r) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} T_i \alpha_i \mathbf{c}_i, \quad T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right), \quad \alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i) $$
where $\delta_j$ is the distance between adjacent samples [S1, unofficial][S2]. The variations lie in:
1.  **Input Representation:** Some methods replace raw coordinates with aggregated image features [S1, unofficial], sparse voxel coordinates [S1, unofficial], or canonical space embeddings [S4].
2.  **Network Topology:** Modifications include splitting the network into separate sampling and shading components [S1, unofficial], increasing depth with residual blocks [S1, unofficial], adding convolutional post-processing [S1, unofficial], or using hypernetworks to generate weights [S1, unofficial].
3.  **Output Heads:** Some architectures output feature vectors for downstream CNNs [S1, unofficial], [SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) values for geometric reasoning [S3], or modulation parameters for generative models [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [AdaNeRF](6195-adanerf.md)
[AdaNeRF](#6195-adanerf.md) decouples the [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) into a lightweight Sampling Network and a heavier Shading Network to achieve real-time rendering by reducing the number of evaluated samples. The Sampling Network predicts importance weights for fixed candidate positions along a ray in a single forward pass. The Shading Network then evaluates only the top-$K$ most significant samples, significantly lowering computational cost compared to standard uniform or [stratified sampling](#1557-stratified-sampling.md). It is chosen when inference speed is critical and geometric ambiguity is not the primary constraint. See [AdaNeRF](6195-adanerf.md).

### [SfMNeRF](8664-sfmnerf.md)
[SfMNeRF](#8664-sfmnerf.md) integrates Structure-from-Motion (SfM) constraints, specifically epipolar geometry and matched SIFT features, into the [training loop](#4290-training-loop.md) to improve reconstruction from sparse inputs. Unlike standard NeRF which relies on photometric consistency alone, SfMNeRF explicitly constrains 3D structure, reducing geometric ambiguity and preventing local minima. It is chosen for sparse-view scenarios where camera poses are known but geometric reconstruction is unstable. See [SfMNeRF](8664-sfmnerf.md).

### [DASNeRF](8668-dasnerf.md)
[DASNeRF](#8668-dasnerf.md) improves 3D reconstruction from sparse views by integrating monocular depth priors (e.g., from DepthAnythingV2) and a dynamic sampling strategy. It enforces depth consistency through a Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss and uses a 5D vector (spatial + ray info) fused at every MLP layer to guide learning. It is chosen when accurate geometry is required from sparse inputs and external depth estimators are available. See [DASNeRF](8668-dasnerf.md).

### [R2L (Neural Light Field)](8670-r2l-neural-light-field.md)
[R2L](#8670-r2l-neural-light-field.md) is a deep neural light field network that distills knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF teacher into an 88-layer deep MLP with extensive residual blocks. It trades width for depth under a fixed FLOPs budget to achieve higher rendering quality and faster inference than standard NeRF. Unlike depth-dependent methods, it does not require ground-truth depth, making it effective for reflective surfaces. It is chosen for high-quality, fast inference from a pre-trained model. See [R2L (Neural Light Field)](8670-r2l-neural-light-field.md).

### [AligNeRF](8695-alignerf.md)
AligNeRF modifies the NeRF architecture to handle high-resolution images and misalignment from moving objects or calibration errors. It combines a convolution-augmented architecture (outputting feature maps processed by a CNN) with a staged, alignment-aware fine-tuning procedure using patch-based sampling and optical flow. It is chosen for high-resolution settings where local neighborhood information and robustness to misalignment are required. See [AligNeRF](8695-alignerf.md).

### [HyperNeRFGAN](8765-hypernerfgan.md)
[HyperNeRFGAN](#8765-hypernerfgan.md) is a generative model that uses a hypernetwork to generate the weights of a simplified NeRF target network from a Gaussian noise vector. It omits viewing direction inputs and uses a standard 2D discriminator, solving 3D-aware image generation when camera positions are unavailable. It is chosen for 3D-aware synthesis in domains like medical imaging or limited-view datasets. See [HyperNeRFGAN](8765-hypernerfgan.md).

### [Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning](8776-mega-nerf-spatial-partitioning.md)
[Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning](#8776-mega-nerf-spatial-partitioning.md) addresses memory and training bottlenecks by decomposing the scene into spatial cells, each managed by a separate MLP submodule trained in parallel. It assigns query points to the nearest centroid and prunes irrelevant training data based on visibility, reducing per-submodule dataset sizes. It is chosen for large-scale scenes where monolithic NeRF training is infeasible. See [Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning](8776-mega-nerf-spatial-partitioning.md).

### [MultiPlaneNeRF](8875-multiplanenerf.md)
[MultiPlaneNeRF](#8875-multiplanenerf.md) replaces the trainable 3D MLP representation with a non-trainable, image-based representation. It projects 3D points onto a fixed set of 2D training images to create an aggregate feature vector, processed by a small, shared implicit decoder. This allows the decoder to generalize across many objects, enabling new view synthesis for unseen objects by swapping input images without retraining. It is chosen for generalization across multiple objects rather than single-scene optimization. See [MultiPlaneNeRF](8875-multiplanenerf.md).

### [Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation](8876-sparse-radiance-field-srf-representation.md)
The Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) is a voxel-based representation that encodes density and radiance into a sparse 3D grid stored in Coordinate Format (COO). It enables direct mesh extraction via Marching Cubes and faster optimization through sparse data structures, serving as an efficient alternative to continuous MLPs. It is chosen when explicit geometry extraction or memory efficiency is prioritized over the flexibility of continuous fields. See [Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation](8876-sparse-radiance-field-srf-representation.md).

### SinNeRF
SinNeRF is a method that uses a depth map to constrain unobserved views via adversarial and perceptual losses [S1, unofficial]. It constructs a semi-supervised learning process with specific semantic and [geometric regularization](#4970-geometric-and-normal-alignment-losses.md) to build a universal 3D model from a single image [S1, unofficial].

### NeRF in the Wild
NeRF in the Wild adds an Appearance embedding to express different lighting conditions and a Transient embedding to model changing geometry [S1, unofficial]. This allows the model to handle unconstrained photo collections with inconsistent lighting and dynamic content [S1, unofficial].

### StyleNeRF
StyleNeRF is a 3D-aware generative model that merges 3D scene representation with style-based generative models [S2]. It uses NeRF to generate low-resolution feature maps and samples them to high resolution to avoid super-computation volume rendering, applying regularization terms to improve 3D consistency [S2].

### CLIP-NeRF
CLIP-NeRF adds a CLIP (text-image pre-trained multimodal model) to provide greater freedom in shape operations and global deformation using a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture [S2]. It applies a learned deformation network to shape modulation, embeds appearance codes into volume rendering, and allows control over both shape and appearance [S2].

### NeRF-RPN
NeRF-RPN uses a multi-scale Object-NeRF architecture where the scene branch encodes geometry and appearance via a voxel representation of 3D neural volume features, and the object branch encodes each independent object [S2]. It allows for 3D bounding box regression directly in NeRF without rendering [S2].

### JacobiNeRF
JacobiNeRF synthesizes a NeRF model based on second-order information (Jacobian matrix) to maximize mutual information between highly correlated entities under random scene perturbations [S2]. The rendering equation is $\hat{C}(r, z_s, z_c) = \sum_{i=1}^{N_c-1} c_i \alpha_i \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$, where $a_i = 1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)$ [S2].

### DE-NeRF
DE-NeRF decomposes lighting, geometry, and appearance to allow relighting of high-frequency environments and appearance editing [S3]. It trains a signed distance field (SDF) function, decomposes the scene into geometric and appearance features (diffuse, roughness, specular), and uses MLPs to predict these properties, integrating them to calculate final color [S3].

### RefSR-NeRF
RefSR-NeRF is a reference-guided super-resolution framework combining NeRF and RefSR-CNN [S3]. It modifies NeRF sampling to patch ray sampling on high-resolution inputs to get low-resolution images, then uses RefSR-CNN to fuse detail-dominant and degradation-dominant feature maps to reconstruct high-resolution images [S3].

### RelightingNeRF
RelightingNeRF handles unstructured photographs and free-viewpoint reconstruction by changing the model architecture to output SDF values and latent features [S3]. It obtains normals, shadow cues, and specular cues from SDF values, then uses a second MLP with sampling positions, lighting positions, and viewing directions to produce the final color [S3].

### DiffusioNeRF
DiffusioNeRF utilizes a denoising diffusion model to learn priors for scene geometry and color, normalizing the geometry and color of the scene to achieve better quality under sparse input views [S3]. It renders random RGBD patches during training and backpropagates estimated gradients of the log-likelihood to the color and density fields [S3].

### GeoNeRF
GeoNeRF is a model with two parts: a geometric morphology reasoner and a renderer [S2]. The reasoner builds a cascaded cost volume for source view sequences, and the renderer infers geometric and appearance representations using a Transformer-based attention mechanism and cascaded cost volumes, then renders fine images using volume rendering [S2].

### Canonical Radiance Field with Voxel Grid
Canonical Radiance Field with Voxel Grid replaces the heavy MLP in NeRF with a learnable voxel radiance feature grid and a lightweight MLP to allow querying finite 3D points in canonical space [S4]. The canonical radiance field is defined as $\Vgrid {R}{Can} = \RadNet (\Vgrid {p}{Can}, \Vgrid {Rf}{Can})$, where $\Vgrid {R}{Can}$ consists of density voxel grid $V\sigma$ and color feature voxel grid $Vcf$ [S4].

## Background
The original NeRF architecture, introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 [S1, unofficial][S2], established the paradigm of implicit [neural representations](#10-neural-and-primitive-based-representations.md) for 3D scenes. However, its reliance on a single deep MLP for every query point led to high computational costs and sensitivity to sparse or noisy inputs [S1, unofficial][S2]. Subsequent research focused on architectural modifications to address these issues. Early extensions like NeRF in the Wild [S1, unofficial] introduced embeddings for lighting and transient objects. Later works explored voxel-based representations [S1, unofficial][S4], generative frameworks [S1, unofficial][S2], and hybrid CNN-MLP architectures [S1, unofficial][S3] to improve speed, generalization, and robustness. The field has evolved from single-scene optimization to large-scale, dynamic, and generative modeling [S1, unofficial][S2, S3].
